summary: Specifies the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism for PIM sparse-style multicast protocols. BSR is one way for a multicast router to learn the group-to-Rendezvous-Point mappings it needs in order to work. Candidate routers advertise themselves and an elected bootstrap router distributes the information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5059 defines how multicast routers agree on which Rendezvous Points serve which groups. Routers elect a Bootstrap Router, which gathers candidates and distributes the resulting mappings.

questions: how do routers learn rendezvous points
how is the bootstrap router elected
how does pim bsr distribute rp mappings
subtitle: How PIM routers elect a Bootstrap Router to collect and distribute group-to-Rendezvous-Point mappings.

tldr.problem: Routers in a PIM domain need consistent mappings from multicast groups to Rendezvous Points. Maintaining the same mappings through manual configuration does not adapt well to failures.
tldr.mechanism: Candidate-BSRs elect a Bootstrap Router. Candidate-RPs advertise their group ranges to it, and the BSR distributes a selected RP-Set to routers in the domain.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5059 replaces RFC 2362 for BSR, updates RFC 4601 and adds support for administrative scope zones. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 5059 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2362 and updates RFC 4601. It has since been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

sections.title: Why Routers Need Group-to-RP Mappings
sections.content:
In PIM sparse-mode and bidirectional PIM, routers need to map multicast group addresses to Rendezvous Points (RPs). Each RP is the root of a distribution tree for a group. Routers in a domain must use consistent mappings so senders can reach the group's receivers.

Routers keep these mappings in an RP-Set. Static configuration can provide the set, but the RFC says it generally does not scale well or adapt to router and link failures. The Bootstrap Router mechanism elects a router to collect RP candidates and distribute mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast routers need to agree on which RP serves each group. BSR automates the collection and distribution of those mappings instead of requiring every router to be configured separately.

sections.title: The BSR Process
sections.content:
The mechanism has four phases, which may overlap. First, Candidate-BSRs send Bootstrap messages and routers use them to elect one BSR. Second, Candidate-RPs send advertisements to that BSR, listing the group ranges they can serve.

Third, the BSR selects a set of candidates. It should avoid a set too large to distribute or so small that it concentrates the load, and it should avoid changing the set frequently. Fourth, the BSR includes the RP-Set in Bootstrap messages that routers flood across the domain.

Routers add received mappings to those they obtain from other sources and let the PIM routing protocol calculate the final group-to-RP mapping. If a network partitions, each part can elect a BSR; after the network reconnects, another election occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers elect one BSR, candidate RPs tell it which groups they can serve, and the BSR distributes a selected list. Routers then use that list with their other mapping information.

sections.title: Administrative Scope Zones
sections.content:
An administrative scope zone is a configured region in which certain multicast groups do not cross the boundary. A Zone Border Router prevents the scoped traffic from entering or leaving that zone. Routers inside the same zone need mappings to RPs within that zone.

RFC 5059 runs a separate BSR mechanism for each scope zone, alongside a non-scoped BSR for groups across the whole PIM domain. Each zone needs at least one Candidate-BSR and at least one Candidate-RP for its scoped addresses. Routers learn about zones from Bootstrap messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A scope zone limits where selected multicast groups can travel. Each zone has its own BSR election and RP mappings, while a separate BSR handles groups without administrative scope.

sections.title: Electing a Bootstrap Router
sections.content:
Each BSR has a weight made from its BSR Priority and IP address. The higher weight wins. A Candidate-BSR can be in Candidate-BSR, Pending-BSR or Elected-BSR state. Pending-BSR is temporary and helps prevent the election from changing rapidly while routers compare candidates.

A non-candidate router accepts Bootstrap messages according to its state. In Accept Any, it accepts the first message. In Accept Preferred, it accepts messages from the current BSR or a candidate with a higher weight. Before processing a message, the router checks that it came from a directly connected neighbor with active PIM Hello state and passed the routing and scope checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Candidate-BSRs compare priority and address to determine which one is preferred. A temporary pending state gives routers time to settle on the elected BSR.

sections.title: Candidate-RP Advertisements and RP-Set Creation
sections.content:
Candidate-RPs periodically send Candidate-RP-Advertisement messages to the BSR for each scope zone. Each advertisement gives the RP's priority, a holdtime and the group ranges it offers. When a new BSR is elected, a Candidate-RP must send one to three advertisements with randomized delays; the RFC recommends three.

The BSR accepts ranges for scope zones where it is elected, or for the non-scoped domain when it is the non-scoped BSR. It stores each mapping until its holdtime expires and builds an RP-Set. If both BIDIR and PIM-SM candidates offer the same range, the BSR includes only one protocol; the recommended default is to prefer BIDIR.
sections.plainLanguage: Candidate-RPs tell the BSR which groups they can serve and how long that offer lasts. The BSR filters and selects those offers to build the RP-Set.

sections.title: Bootstrap and Candidate-RP Messages
sections.content:
BSR uses two PIM message types: type 4 for Bootstrap and type 8 for Candidate-RP-Advertisement. PIM messages use IP protocol number 103. Candidate-RP advertisements are unicast to the BSR. Bootstrap messages are normally multicast with TTL 1 to ALL-PIM-ROUTERS: 224.0.0.13 for IPv4 and ff02::d for IPv6.

A Bootstrap message carries the BSR identity and priority, a hash-mask length and group ranges with their RP addresses, priorities and holdtimes. If the message is too large for a packet, it can be sent as semantic fragments. Routers update a group's mapping only after receiving the RP information for that range; a missing fragment therefore affects the ranges it carried.
sections.plainLanguage: Bootstrap messages distribute BSR and RP-Set information, while Candidate-RP messages carry offers to the BSR. Large Bootstrap messages can be split so losing one fragment does not invalidate every group mapping.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
The default BS_Period is 60 seconds, so the BSR normally sends Bootstrap messages at that interval. The default BS_Timeout is 130 seconds; if no message arrives by then, routers time out the BSR. Bootstrap messages must be sent at least 10 seconds apart by default.

The default SZ_Timeout is 1300 seconds for forgetting a scope zone with no Bootstrap messages. Candidate-RP advertisements normally repeat every 60 seconds, with a randomized backoff from 0 to 3 seconds after a new BSR is elected. The RFC also specifies that the Bootstrap timeout must exceed the message period and the scope-zone timeout must exceed the Bootstrap timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: Timers determine how often the BSR announces mappings and how long routers wait before forgetting a BSR or scope zone. These timeouts are longer than the regular message intervals.

sections.title: Security Risks and Defenses
sections.content:
An attacker who changes Bootstrap messages or advertises as a Candidate-RP could stop multicast traffic from reaching receivers, divert it for monitoring or flood a third party. The RFC recommends limiting which source addresses the BSR accepts Candidate-RP advertisements from and providing per-interface controls for sending and accepting Bootstrap messages.

Other defenses include filtering spoofed source addresses, rate-limiting PIM messages by message type and, where needed, using IPsec authentication between PIM routers or for Candidate-RP advertisements. Rate limits should treat message types independently so a flood of one type does not prevent delivery of another.
sections.plainLanguage: False BSR or Candidate-RP messages can redirect or disrupt multicast traffic. The RFC recommends checking message sources, controlling where messages are accepted and using authentication when needed.
